Complete Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences / event-study with a triple-difference extension.  

• Unit of observation: individual 17- to 22-year-olds in CPS-October, NLSY-79, HS&B, SIPP or state administrative files.  
• Treatment: introduction (or large dollar expansion) of state-level college-cost-reduction programs between 1980 and 2010.  Programs are coded by design features:  

 A. “Simple, universal merit” (e.g., GA HOPE, WV PROMISE)  
 B. “Need-based, high complexity” (federal Pell, Cal Grant before 2000, FAFSA-only)  
 C. “Need-based + services / incentives” (Opening Doors, DC TAG, STAR, Upward Bound pilots)  

Because states introduced (and sometimes later modified) these programs at different times, staggered adoption creates plausibly exogenous within-state shocks to the college price faced by successive high-school cohorts.  

Why DiD?  
• The policy shocks are discrete, dateable and occur at the state level; most students do not anticipate them several years in advance.  
• The data span many untreated states and long pre- and post-periods, letting us test for pre-trends and implement modern staggered-adoption estimators (Callaway-Sant’Anna 2021, Sun & Abraham 2021).  

Triple-difference:  The main DiD compares low-income students (family income < 200 % of poverty) to higher-income peers within the same state‐year, adding a second difference that nets out contemporaneous factors affecting enrollment for everyone.  

Secondary checks: For programs with sharp eligibility cut-offs (e.g., Cal Grant GPA ≥ 3.0 & income < $61K; Pell EFC ≤ 0), we will run fuzzy RDDs as “within-program audits” of the DiD findings.  

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment indicator T_{ist} = 1 if individual i in state s belongs to the first high-school graduation cohort that faced the lower net price created by a program of type d.  

Control groups  
• Across states: otherwise‐similar students in states that have not yet adopted the program.  
• Within states (triple diff): higher-income students who remain ineligible for the aid even after adoption.  

Timing The event date is the academic year in which the first graduating class could use the scholarship (e.g., GA HOPE: fall 1993 incoming freshmen). We assign treatment by expected high-school graduation year to avoid endogenous gap-years.  

No running variable is needed for the main DiD. (Running variables appear only in the auxiliary RDDs.)  

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: absent the policy, low-income students in adopting states would have followed the same enrollment/completion trend as their low-income peers in non-adopting states (and as higher-income students in their own state).  
 Plausibility:  Pre-treatment event-study coefficients will be presented.  Large national datasets over 10–15 pre years allow visual/ statistical checks.  

A2. No simultaneous confounders that differentially affect low-income students exactly when a state adopts the scholarship (e.g., K-12 reforms, minimum-wage hikes).  
 Plausibility:  We include state-year controls for unemployment, minimum wage, K-12 finance reforms, and tuition changes at public 2- and 4-year colleges.  

A3. Stable composition: the share of low-income high-school graduates is not abruptly altered by the policy (no strategic grade retention).  
 Plausibility:  October CPS lets us test for sudden discontinuities in high-school graduation counts.  

A4. Limited migration: families do not move across state lines solely to capture the program in significant numbers.  
 Plausibility:  ACS and IRS migration tables show very small interstate mobility for 17- to 18-year-olds.  We will replicate results restricting to individuals who lived in the same state 5 years earlier.  

================================================================  
4. Major Threats and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Selective in-state tuition changes that accompany the scholarship  
 • Include college-level IPEDS tuition × state-year fixed effects in the model.  
 • Instrument tuition with lagged appropriations to separate price from aid.  

2. Treatment heterogeneity and staggered adoption bias under two-way FE.  
 • Use Callaway-Sant’Anna and Sun-Abraham estimators rather than simple TWFE.  
 • Report “stacked” DiD where each treated state is compared only to not-yet-treated states.  

3. Measurement error in income (CPS) that blurs low- vs high-income status.  
 • Re-define income groups using multiple thresholds (150 %, 200 %, 250 % of poverty) and show robustness.  
 • In state administrative data, use free/reduced-price lunch status from high-school records.  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
################################################################################
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)        # fast data handling
library(fixest)            # TWFE & Sun-Abraham
library(did)               # Callaway-Sant'Anna
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)
library(rdrobust)          # For auxiliary RDDs
################################################################################
# 1. Load and merge CPS-October files already harmonised to cps_oct.csv
cps <- fread("cps_oct.csv")   # one row = individual

# 2. Key variables -------------------------------------------------------------
cps[, lowinc  := as.integer(family_income < 2 * poverty_threshold)]
cps[, treated := 0L]     # initialise

# program adoption dates (illustrative)
adopt <- data.table(state = c("GA","WV","AR","MA","DC"),
                    adopt_year = c(1993,2002,1991,2005,2000),
                    type = c("HOPE","PROMISE","AR_Sch","Adams","DCTAG"))

cps <- merge(cps, adopt, by = "state", all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicator: first cohort affected = grad_year >= adopt_year
cps[, treated := as.integer(grad_year >= adopt_year & !is.na(adopt_year))]

# 3. Basic DiD (Sun-Abraham) ---------------------------------------------------
es_sa <- feols(enrolled ~ sunab(adopt_year, year) * lowinc | 
                         state + year,
               data = cps,
               cluster = ~state)

iplot(es_sa, xlab = "Years relative to adoption", main = "Event study")

# 4. Callaway–Sant’Anna triple difference -------------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname   = "enrolled",
             tname   = "year",
             idname  = "id",
             gname   = "adopt_year",
             xformla = ~ lowinc + age + female + black + hispanic,
             data    = cps[lowinc == 1],   # restrict to low-income if desired
             est_method = "dr")

agg_effect <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effect)
ggdid(agg_effect)

# 5. Robustness: Remove states with simultaneous tuition cuts ------------------
cps_rob <- cps[!(state %in% c("TN","FL"))]  # example exclusions
es_rob <- feols(enrolled ~ sunab(adopt_year, year) * lowinc | state + year,
                data = cps_rob, cluster = ~state)

# 6. Auxiliary RDD for Cal Grant (fuzzy RD) ------------------------------------
cal <- fread("calgrant_admin.csv")  # state admin data
rd <- rdrobust(y = cal$enrolled,
               x = cal$gpa,        # running variable
               c = 3.0,            # GPA cutoff
               fuzzy = cal$award>0)

print(rd)
################################################################################
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (human-capital with borrowing constraints) predicts a positive enrollment and completion response when college prices fall for liquidity-constrained families. From prior literature, I expect:  

• Simple merit or need-based grants: +4–6 p.p. on first-year enrollment among low-income high-school grads (baseline ≈ 50 %).  
• Programs that bundle mandatory counseling/learning communities: an additional +2 p.p. persistence into year 2 and +1–1.5 p.p. six-year completion relative to “money-only” programs.  
I do not expect sizable effects on higher-income students, so the triple-difference estimate should be of similar magnitude to the raw DiD.  

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Common pre-treatment trends ………… 1  
C2: No anticipation / timing exogeneity …… 0.8  
C3: No simultaneous confounders ………… 0.7  
C4: Stable composition / no sorting ………… 0.9  
C5: Correct treatment timing & exposure … 1  

 Average score ≈ 0.88 ⇒ research design is reasonably credible but must document timing and confounder checks thoroughly.
